This is a folk story with no scientific basis, but it is still a compelling example of how we all interpret reality, regardless of our sophisticated, knowledgeable facade. A few years ago, I received an email describing an interesting experiment that took place at an American university:

A team of students, half dressed in white T-shirts and the other half in black were told to pass around a basketball. The task of the spectator observing the short film was to count how many times the ball was passed from a student with a white T-shirt to another student wearing a white T-shirt. You can stop reading here and check it out for yourself. Just scan the QR code and follow the instructions. Spoiler Alert! Do not continue reading until you have experienced this test for yourself. Like you just did, I pressed “Play,” and the students started running around the room, passing the ball. After about 15 seconds, the film ends, and the question appears: “How many passes did you count?” You enter the number you counted. Then another, stranger question appears: “Did you see anything unexpected in the room during the experiment?” No, I hadn’t. “Is it possible that a big black gorilla came into the room and waved hello to you?” What?? No gorilla came!

“So now, please observe the same clip again, this time without counting.” Doing as I was told, I pressed “Play,” this time without counting, simply observing. To my astonishment, a student dressed in a black gorilla costume appeared from the right side of the frame, stood in the middle of the room, waved a big hello, and left from the left side! No tricks or technological wizardry. All the confusion was created by my own mind. To succeed in the given task, my mind filtered out everything irrelevant to its mission at that moment—including a gorilla saying hello. Truly incredible. No gorilla. It was simply brushed out of the picture by my mind. There is a book written about this experiment and its conclusions called "The Invisible Gorilla" by Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons.

What do we learn from all of this? Our mind is a problematic instrument. It creates a limited, partial, and distorted picture of the reality that is happening every moment. This means that the way we interact with reality will almost always be based on a partial and therefore inaccurate picture. You see, our perception of reality is so subjective. What is the point of arguing about whether the gorilla is beautiful or not if I see a gorilla and you don’t? Science, as well as spiritual teachers, teaches us that reality is much more complex than what we allow ourselves to grasp or experience. The spiritual path encourages the seeker to develop their mind to perceive finer levels of reality. Awakening or enlightenment can be described, in this sense, as being able to hold in and fully experience 400 billion bits of information at any given moment—to actually know, experience, and be what truly is. Mind - The Thoughts Upon the screen of the mind, an endless continuum of emotions, thoughts, and sensations is projected.

This continuum is not a problem. It becomes a problem when we become entangled in it and believe it, identify with it. You sit for meditation. Hands are in the correct position. You adopt a serene expression. Eyes are closed. A content smile. All seems well. Half an hour later, you report: “It didn’t work out.” Why not? “Because I had thoughts clouding my mind.” Meditation is all about NON-DOERSHIP So? Why is that a problem? Meditation is not about banishing all thoughts and sensations—a forced silencing of the mind. Many of us, even those who have been on a spiritual path for years, go astray at this point. Trying to banish the mind is a form of doing. And meditation is about non-doing. Meditation means peacefully observing the film projected on the screen of the mind, with all its content, without rejection, manipulation, or personal interest.

Upon the screen of my mind, a thought is projected. I do not believe it—I merely observe. Now there is a thought reminding me of what that person said to me earlier in the day. Now, a thought planning what I should say to them next time. I just observe… Now, a thought trying to convince me to stop this “useless” observation of thoughts passing on the screen of the mind, trying to induce doubt. So what? I only observe. I do not get carried away by it. I do not respond. I do not believe it. I do not identify with it. That is the quality of a mature consciousness. Andrew Cohen, an American teacher, once shared an experience from one of his lectures to emphasize this point. He was at a student forum at a university in the US. During the Q&A, a very attractive student asked a question. Andrew said that he couldn’t hear the question at all. The only thought in his mind was: “Wow, what a stunning woman! I wouldn’t mind having a go with her…”

He uses this as a spiritual teaching—an example of true freedom from the mind. The thought itself, he explained, was not a problem at all. It is normal and even expected for such thoughts to arise in a man’s mind when meeting an attractive person. A moment ago, that thought was in the mind of the person to his left, and the next moment it will travel on to distract someone else. This is simply the nature of thought. It becomes a problem if he chooses to believe the thought, to get carried away by it, to identify with it, and to react to it. “If this thought came into my head, it probably means I need to do something about it. Maybe I’ll try to contact this woman during the break. Maybe I can get some benefit from it.”

Or, it would become a problem if he built a judgmental relationship with the thought, along the lines of: “I am a spiritual teacher. Spiritual teachers are not supposed to have thoughts like that. Thoughts like that should not appear in the minds of spiritual teachers at all. Maybe I am an imposter. Maybe I should refrain from teaching for a while.” (Which he eventually did, a few years later…) As long as he does not succumb to this kind of influence from thoughts, they have no power over him. They have no power at all. They are only events projected onto the screen of the mind. So, at this stage, I would encourage you to practice this mindfulness exercise: Observe the relationship you have with your thoughts. What happens within you when a thought appears? How do you react to it? Do you tend to get carried away by its appearance? Do you believe it and entangle yourself with it? Do you turn yourself into its slave? Make yourself available for this observation. By observing a thought without accepting it as truth, you can come to understand a fundamental reality.

Thoughts have no power. No power at all. Unless you believe them. Wake up and realize this. You may now say to yourself: “But I was told that my thoughts are very important; they create my reality…” This is a common misunderstanding. What influences your reality is your intention (Sankalpa), not your thoughts. Intention originates from the Being (Self); thought originates from the Intellect. These are two very different entities. We will discuss this further later in the book. Mind - Emotions Emotions can become our masters. Even on the spiritual path, we hear teachers telling us to “Follow your heart.” But how can the heart lead us? When you let your awareness be carried away by your emotions, following every whim of the heart, you are lost. Today you feel one way, tomorrow another. “I’m sad; let me stay in bed. I’m happy; it’s not the time to attend to my duties.” Emotions come and go constantly. We believe them blindly and let them take control.

A free consciousness recognizes emotions as events projected onto the screen of the mind, just like thoughts and sensations, and does not believe them. A free consciousness is like the lens of a movie projector. It allows the projected light to pass through to the screen, free of distortions or flaws. The lens has no personal interest. It does not care if a horror show, a drama, or a comedy is currently playing. Its only concern is its duty: to transmit the light to the screen. So may you. Become that lens. Allow the great light to spread upon the world through you—clean, distortion-free, and transparent. A free consciousness is a consciousness that knows: I am not my Mind. The Mind is the screen on which my experiences are projected. Practice: Clear some time for a quiet experience of the Mind. Take a deep breath in… and let go. Link to a guided meditation about the MIND: The Intellect Fourth Level of Existence The Intellect is not who I am. It is the movie critic – judging the movie and criticizing it, filling it with the meaning of “right” and “wrong”

The Intellect is the fourth level in which we all exist. If the mind is the screen on which the movie of your experiences is projected, then the intellect is the movie critic. It decides whether the book you are currently reading is good or bad. You find the sum of your experiences on the screen of the mind. The mind collects the information transmitted by the body, adds the phenomena it finds in our inner world, and assembles it into a compiled experience we refer to as reality. We have already discussed the limitations of the mind as a precise instrument for creating an authentic picture of reality. The intellect takes the fractured picture created by the mind and gives it an amazing addition: it gives it meaning. “Sitting is good. Sitting is right/ moral/ desirable/ valuable/ beneficial…” The intellect is the prism through which we interpret the world around us.

A baby observes the world without any judgment or preconditioning. It simply observes what is there. As we grow older, we add interpretation to this pure observation. Any added interpretation further distorts what is actually there and takes us further from the opportunity to innocently experience the object of our observation. A tree will never be simply a tree through the prism of the intellect. It will become another opportunity to judge and categorize: “Beautiful tree/ very tall tree/ an oak tree/ an old tree/ what is this tree doing here? Someone needs to cut it down, it’s blocking my view…” Innocent eyes allow a clean observation of what truly is there, without preconditions or judgment. You might ask: “What were all these years of learning and accumulating knowledge good for if real wisdom is about observing life with childlike innocence, with no past impressions?” That is a great question. Again and again, on the spiritual path, we meet teachers who remind us that we learn so that we have something to forget. How can you let go if there is nothing to let go of?

If you have a judgmental intellect, use it, but don’t get hung up on it. The intellect is where most of the obstacles on the path to true freedom are born, so we will address it more thoroughly. Intellect and Human Suffering The first space we will investigate is the gap where all our suffering is born and raised. What is suffering? Suffering is the experience that creates stress and contraction within you. When you are frustrated, angry, and violent, you feel bitter, disappointed, and deterred, it is difficult to forgive and accept— You are suffering.

Where was your suffering born? Your intellect is the generator and home of your suffering. What is the origin of suffering? Many teachers have dedicated entire philosophies to answering this question. It is worthwhile to study it in depth (just so you will have something to forget later…). You can, for example, search online for “Four Noble Truths” and find thousands of articles describing what Buddha taught about suffering more than 2,600 years ago. The subject of suffering is so fundamental to human experience that any opportunity to minimize it is an invitation for true transformation—one that fundamentally changes the way we live. The following sentence is such an invitation. If you agree to live according to it, you will inevitably realize a transformation in your life. The following sentence is not meant to change your life unless you belong to those (special ones) who are willing to change their lives based on a single sentence: That is all.

It is so simple that it may overwhelm you. “That can’t be right!” you might say to yourself. “Life is not so simple. Can it be so simple? What’s the trick?” No trick. It really is very simple. Do you wish to minimize the suffering in your life? Minimize the gap! Return to what is. I am not calling for a zombie-like life, devoid of ambition, passive and apathetic. On the contrary, this is a call for full engagement with life—one that arises from an accepting and willing attitude, a place that does not reject or avoid, free of conflict or stress, and ultimately, full of love. Wake up and see: your suffering appears each time your intellect creates a gap between what is happening right now and what it believes should have happened instead. So, at this point, I encourage you to practice this mindfulness exercise: When you feel stress accumulating in your body, breath, or mind, stop momentarily and recognize the gap. Give it a name. It will always be there. Always! This practice is very important. List all those occasions where you suffered and the gap you found that gave birth to them.

Who are you frustrated or angry at? What did they do or not do? What do you believe they should have done? If there’s a gap between them - you suffer! For example, your knee hurts—this is an undisputed fact. Do you reject the pain? Do you believe the pain should disappear before you can be happy again? If you do - you suffer! Pain is inevitable - Suffering is optional Pain and suffering are not the same. Pain is the phenomenon you are invited to experience in a given moment. The scene is currently projected on the screen of the mind. If your intellect labels it as negative, harmful, or obsolete, you add suffering to the pain. You suffer. Pain itself is not a problem. It is merely a request from the body for attention to a specific area. “Something is s3tuck over there. Please pay attention.” But you prefer to ignore or suppress that request because the intellect labels it as uncomfortable, thus undesirable = bad. So, you are in pain and you suffer.

Pain can be a source of growth. On the spiritual path, pain can be an instrument to come closer to the divine. Sadhus in India sometimes experience divine upliftment through physical pain. Western religions also use self-mortification as a means of inner cleansing and unification with the Divine. Pain is not a problem. It is just a sensation (phenomena) currently experienced in the mind. Let me tell you a story: A person is involved in a car accident, God forbid. He wakes up in the ER and the doctor asks how he feels. The person replies: “Doc, I can’t feel my legs; my whole body is in pain, but there’s no pain in my legs.” The doctor takes a needle and pricks the toe, but the person feels no pain. Now, is that good or bad? Every morning, the doctor comes with the needle, but still no pain. After two weeks, the doctor shows up again with the needle, and this time—surprise—the person jumps in pain. “Ouch! It hurts!” Now, is that good or bad? A year later, the person mows their lawn and steps on a thorn; the same prick at the same toe; the exact same pain. Now, is that good or bad?

The pain is the same. It is the interpretation, the context, that makes it “good” or “bad.” That translation happens in the intellect, where human suffering is born and raised. A free consciousness avoids this discrimination between good and bad. Or, at least it does not believe them when they appear. There is no ultimate good or bad What’s good for you may be bad for me. What was good for you yesterday may be bad for you today. The present moment comes to us with no built-in signs of plus (+) or minus (–). It becomes one or the other in the eyes of the beholder (or their intellect). You could say that the present moment has no regard for the experiencer. It will never try to please them. It doesn’t take their opinion into account. It cannot please everyone. (In that sense, the present moment can teach us an important lesson: live your life and let go of the idea that you might be able to please everyone around you. It is not possible). The present moment is inevitable

The present moment has only one obligation, not to you but to creation, and that divine obligation is to happen. And that is precisely what it has been doing since the beginning of time. From the moment time was born until the moment time ends, the present moment happens. Your intellect decides if it is good or bad, beneficial or harmful, desirable or redundant. If it is impossible for you to experience the world in its holistic totality, and you must divide your reality into duality, it is preferable to avoid the discrimination of “good” and “bad”. Instead, you can divide the world into “knowledge” versus “ignorance”. Are you driven by knowledge or blinded by ignorance? Ignorance can always be filled with knowledge. Darkness can always be dispelled by light. In Genesis, chapter 2, it is described how God placed us in the Garden of Eden, saying: “…Eat your fill from all of the garden’s trees; but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

God said: “I have created this for you. Do as you please. Just avoid one thing: avoid the tree of knowledge of good and bad.” In other words: “I will determine what is good or bad. You don’t need to bother.” But Adam believed he knew better about what was good and what was bad. He wanted to be the one deciding these matters. So, he was tempted to taste the forbidden fruit. Then God said: “So, you wish to decide what is good or bad? Then leave this place and go decide outside.” That was the moment we were expelled from paradise. Let go of the idea that the world is divided into good and bad, and realize: you are back in paradise. So, we learned an incredibly important lesson: Suffering is not a destiny. It is not a necessity of life. It is merely how we allow ourselves to experience life. If we agree to narrow the gap between what is actually happening and what we believe should have been, we lessen the suffering in our lives. If you wish, you could close the gap completely and live a life devoid of any shadow of suffering. How to do that?

I suggest a three-step process to awaken beyond suffering: Add Modesty: The intellect tends to be very determined, and very vain. “I know what should have happened.” “You shouldn’t have talked to me like that!” So, the first step is to add modesty: “I don’t truly know. Should this have happened rather than that? I do not know.” Guruji says that the whole spiritual journey is from a very firm “I know” to a very beautiful “I don’t know.”

Adopt the Opposite Paradigm: Adopt the opposite paradigm to the one that initially caused your suffering. Instead of believing the thought: “You shouldn’t have talked to me like that,” now believe the thought: “That is exactly how you should have talked to me.” And how do I know that to be true? Because that is how you talked to me. I am now a lover of the present moment instead of a warrior against it. Some people dedicate their entire lives to arguing with reality, but reality wins 100% of the time. Now, when the paradigm you hold describes reality instead of opposing it, you realize that there is no gap anymore. If there is no gap, there is no suffering. Drop All Paradigms: Drop all paradigms, good and bad. Drop all preconceptions, preconditions, and beliefs. Allow yourself to be completely available to experience the present moment to its fullest. Ultimately, you will dissolve and become the present moment itself. The experiencer melts into the experience, and they become one. Imagine: no more suffering. At all.

The spiritual path is very clear on this point. The ideal it sets is a life devoid of suffering—not to make our suffering more endurable or more humane (that is what psychotherapy is for), but to let go of it altogether. Only then will we be available to live our lives to our fullest potential—a life of renewed responsibility for our presence in this world. In the second chapter, we will learn why it is so important to live a life devoid of suffering. And no, it has nothing to do with personal benefit. Intellect and Your Fears The intellect is where most of our fears are born. Fear is one of the most significant forces that manipulate us all, so it is recommended to become acquainted with it—to learn when it is useful and when it is harmful. Fear is experienced in the first six of the seven levels of existence. That is six, not seven since the seventh level—the Self—is fearless, devoid of fear. How is it possible to grow beyond our fears and be free? First, it is important to differentiate between the two types of fear we all experience: Fear of an immediate danger The other kind

Let’s begin with the first kind of fear. Here, fear itself is not a problem. It actually plays an important role in maintaining order, protecting our environment, and allowing life to flow with balance. It is the power of rejection opposing the power of attraction, which together maintain life in a physical world of matter and energy. Fear is useful when faced with clear and immediate danger Fear is important and beneficial, but only when it alerts us to a concrete and immediate danger existing in the present moment. If a truck is rushing toward you, you had better jump away. If a lion is approaching, take cover. That sort of fear keeps you alive. It is a survival instinct you should listen to. There is no need to eliminate or overcome it. Fear of disease promotes hygienic practices. Fear of chaos maintains order. However, most of the time, we deal with the second type of fear—the fear that does not point to a concrete and immediate danger but to a movie projected in our head. Such movies are born in the intellect.

The intellect takes an impression from the past and projects it into the future of the present. Something happened to me, or to someone I know or have heard of, once in the past, and I take that memory and project it into the future, saying: “God forbid it should happen again.” The consciousness again jumps between the past and the future. We choose to believe that horror movie that is projected into our mind; sometimes we are even addicted to it. Meanwhile, we miss what is happening right now. In words we have already seen, fear can be defined as: Byron Katie, a remarkable woman who developed a method to narrow this gap, met a distressed woman a few years ago. “Please help me; I haven’t been able to sleep for many nights,” the woman said. “Why? What happened?” “My son is about to join the army, and I can’t let go of the idea that he’s going to be abducted by the enemy and tortured in interrogation chambers.” A genuine fear. With much love and compassion, Katie asked: “Tell me, right now, as we’re talking, where is your son?”

“He’s on vacation before his draft, at the beach. He’s with his friends there for the night.” “Notice,” Katie said, “right now, your son is at the beach with his friends, but in your head, he’s being tortured by the enemy. You’re choosing a fictional horror movie in your head over reality. What kind of mother does this behavior make you?” “Insane,” the woman replied. “He doesn’t want to hear from me; he doesn’t reply to my text messages.” “What would you be without believing that movie?” Katie asked. “Sane again,” the woman replied. “My son would return to me.” All that terrible drama is born from a fictional, futuristic thought we choose to hold onto instead of reality. So, what to do with all this? First, just remember: “Fear is merely a movie projected in your head, distracting you from fully experiencing what is really there.” The next time you feel overshadowed by fear, remind yourself that it’s just a movie.

As soon as your consciousness returns to the present moment, it will find that all is well. There is no immediate danger; no lion nearby. It’s okay to relax. Hakuna Matata… So, all you need to do when you encounter fear is take a deep breath in and return to the present moment. Fear in the Body/Breath Fear is also felt as a physical contraction somewhere in the body (just as with suffering). The body reacts to fear by contracting. You can use this contraction to let go of the fear and return to the present moment. Simply put, when fear arises, locate the contraction in your body. It is there somewhere; just be aware and find it. Often, it can be found in the belly, chest, or throat. If we release the physical contraction we find in the body, we will discover that the fear that caused the contraction disappears along with its physical manifestation.

I invite you to try the following mindfulness exercise: If you are feeling afraid of something that is not an immediate threat, close your eyes and locate the areas of contraction in your body. Take a few deep breaths, directing your breath into these areas of tension. As you exhale, imagine releasing some of that contraction. Gradually allow yourself to relax and let go. After about two minutes of this practice, return your focus to your breath and the present moment. You may find that the contraction has diminished along with the fear that triggered it. You are now in a position to embrace what is. Fear in the Mind

In the realm of the mind, fear can be easily recognized as a thought, an idea, or a “bad movie.” When you are trained to observe the thoughts in your mind without believing them, you can simply let go of your grip on the scary thoughts you may be experiencing. Remember, what you give attention to grows. If you keep focusing on your scary thoughts, believing them to be true, you keep feeding them with energy, helping them grow and take over your consciousness, distracting you from what is actually happening right now. What you give attention to - grows Instead, shift your attention back to the present moment. Your presence in the present moment will grow accordingly, and fear will diminish, as you realize there is no clear and immediate danger here and now. Fear in the Intellect There is another tool you can use to deal with fear. Since fear is generated in the intellect, the intellect can also be used to resolve it.

If fear persists, preventing peace of mind, you can investigate its depths and origins. There is a powerful technique for this, which I call “The Leading Question.” A leading question does not have a definite answer, and never will. However, it guides your path of self-development and self-realization. Its importance lies in our willingness to continue asking it, even though we know there will be no single, absolute answer. “Who is God?” “What is love?” “What is the purpose of my life?” and the ultimate question, “Who am I?” are examples of such questions. Our willingness to keep asking them fuels the evolution of human consciousness. An answer to these questions would terminate the investigation, thus emptying the questions of their purpose. Keep asking. Investigate. Learn. Don’t be satisfied by any answer, however convincing it may sound. There can never be, nor will there ever be, a definitive answer to a leading question. What is important is that you dare to keep asking.

For instance, when investigating fear, you might use the leading question: “Why is this so frightening?” Pick a fear—any fear—and begin to investigate: Why is this frightening? Such an investigation might look like this: The rule is that you cannot repeat the same answer twice. If no answer appears, you might want to stay with the question. Let it sink in and do its work. “Why is this so frightening?” Such a process is extremely powerful and precise because it takes you beyond your defenses, straight to the heart of the matter. At this juncture, I encourage you to engage in this mindfulness exercise: Select a fear and investigate it using the Leading Question as outlined. Be candid in your reflections; there is no need to present an altered version of yourself. Allow the Leading Question to guide you toward the essence of your fear. Possible Paths You May Discover From experience, I can say that there are two major paths of investigation that most brave individuals, who dare to investigate fear, may encounter: The first path leads you towards the “Empty Station.”

I’m afraid of A because of B, and of B because of C… and of X because of Y. But now that I’m thinking about it, “Y” doesn’t scare me at all. On the contrary, “Y” intrigues me, and challenges me. When I realize that, I discover that my original fear is just the top floor of a tower hanging in the air. It has no substantial basis that truly threatens me. Deep below this pile of fears, there is an empty station, devoid of fear. Model of Investigation using a Leading Question. Such a discovery has a therapeutic effect when dealing with our fears, as it neutralizes the original fear. The next time you encounter that fear, you will find it has less of an effect on you. It is not as intimidating as before.

However, there is a second path of investigation, a path that leads us to a central station through which most of us pass when investigating our fears. You may find that this path takes you, as described earlier, through fears hiding behind other fears, all the way to the core of the matter: the essence of your fears. The most rooted and basic fear of all, the most intimidating and paralyzing fear, is the fear of losing control. I’m afraid of A because of B, and of B because of C… and of X because of Y, but in Y, I discover that what I am really afraid of is the possibility of losing control. This fear is so deeply rooted in our being, so intimidating, that we often don't dare look it in the eye. We call it by other names, camouflaging it behind more user-friendly, less paralyzing disguises. But it is still there, like a hidden predator, awaiting its chance to consume us and prevent freedom.

Why is it so scary? Why is this fear of losing control so central to our daily conduct? I asked Guruji this question many years ago. Actually, the precise question was: “Guruji, why is it so difficult to let go of our need for control?” Back then, I had already realized that it was a need rather than a necessity, but that knowledge did not help me relax and let go. His reply astounded me. He said: “Yaron, what is it that you believe you have control over?” It took me years to fully realize the depth of this simple answer, but the deeper I investigated it, the clearer the picture of my conduct in life became. What is it that you believe you have control over? Look back at your life from the beginning and search: what do you control? Do you have control over your thoughts? Thoughts come, stay, and leave without permission. Have you ever been able to chase away one thought with another? Try not to think of an apple for a moment… Do you have control over your emotions? Emotions rise, overflowing the screen of your mind; now you are happy, later miserable.

Thoughts, emotions, and sensations pass through this screen like clouds in the sky, with no control whatsoever. You might occasionally choose how you externalize these emotions when you are not overwhelmed by them, but as events, they simply exist on their own. Do you have any control over your body? Your body operates by itself, without any control from your side. It grows, cleans itself, nourishes itself, fights disease and bacteria, and maintains a fine balance of temperature, moisture, acid, and much more. Endless processes occur that you are usually unaware of, let alone in control of.

You want to bend your finger. What happens between your decision to bend it and the actual bending? Do you have any idea? How does it bend? What happens there, without any of your so-called “control”? If you were to control the process, it wouldn’t bend a millimeter. What is happening there, from the moment of deciding to bend a finger to the neurological pulse the brain sends to the nerve, which projects to the muscle, which contracts and bends the finger? Don’t worry; even the best researchers don’t fully understand how an intention translates into an electrical pulse. A control-free mystery. Step out into the world and observe: what do you have control over? The birds are singing; people are passing by; cars are honking; the sun rises and sets. What do you control in all of that?

The world manages itself. Life happens without any control from your side. Look back on your life and examine the major milestones that have shaped it, from day one to the present moment. They all just happened by themselves, without your control. Your family, friends, your profession—they all just appeared along the way, assembled by changing circumstances. So, here is another transformative sentence: You walk through life with clenched fists, protecting an illusion of control, holding so tightly that your fists bleed. Until one of two things happens: you either let go or you die—whichever comes first. In both cases, your fists loosen, your fingers open, and what do you find in them? Emptiness. You are protecting nothing. There is no need to continue fearing the loss of control. All is well. Life simply happens. You can relax.

Many years ago, I had a friend who was a TV producer. A TV producer is often paid to be a control freak. Everything needs to operate with clockwork precision; every second is measured in dollars. Throughout the day, she was connected to two phones, one on each ear, managing everything. We met at a party one day, and she looked like a zombie—like a plant you forgot to water for two weeks. “What happened?” I asked. “I’m so tired of this kind of life,” she replied. “I have no energy to continue this lifestyle. I feel like a farmer sitting on a wagon, holding the reins too tight, needing to know and control exactly where the horse puts its feet with each step. It feels like I have blisters on my hands from gripping so hard,” she said. I gave her a big hug. “Just relax,” I said. “Let go. There’s nothing else to do.”

A week later, we met by chance, and she was radiant. What had happened? “Yaron, I experienced a miracle. In the past week, my life changed. I gave up. I returned from production at 2:00 in the morning, lay down on my bed, and simply gave up. I realized that my life couldn’t continue like this. Your words were ringing in my ears, and I decided to let go. The next day, I went to work, did my best, and let go of my need to control events. And to my astonishment, a few miracles happened. First, I rediscovered the people I had worked with for so long. I found that I love them, and they love me back. Until then, they were just a means to an end - ‘Gofers’. Suddenly, I saw them as the amazing, dedicated colleagues and friends they were!” The farmer lies on the pile of hay in the back of the wagon, lets go of the need for control, and relaxes. Only then does he discover the path the horse is taking. He is now free to enjoy the scenery, the view, the flowers along the way, and the butterfly on the flower.

“And an even bigger miracle happened,” she continued. “I found that when I let go, the job gets done, even better than it would have if I had manipulated the process based on my fear of losing control.” The horse knows a shortcut the farmer was unaware of. If he just relaxes, he can get home even sooner than planned. This is a story I carry with me. Just relax - Let go Life is beautiful; it’s okay to enjoy it. When you loosen your grip and let go of the obsessive need to control events, you discover that your life evolves into a new dimension of freedom and serenity. All the energy previously dedicated to maintaining the illusion of control is now available for a more productive life. You become more creative, at ease with yourself and your surroundings, full of happiness and joy. You discover that life, contrary to what you might expect, becomes full of action, enthusiasm, and joy. So, how do we let go of our need for control? Some will read this book once, be reminded of this truth, and that’s it! The transformation is complete.

Others (most of us belong to this group) will need to be reminded of this truth again and again. For that purpose, spiritual practice was invented. Meditation is first and foremost a practice of letting go of the illusion of control. Events are happening: feelings, sensations, and thoughts cross the screen of the mind without permission, guidance, manipulation, cravings, or aversions. I merely observe the scene, like watching an endless movie over which I have no control. While meditating, consciousness is exposed to this process of control-free observation and becomes accustomed to it. Slowly and gradually, it becomes used to the undisputed fact of the control-free flow of life. And like everything we become used to, this realization stops frightening and controlling us. So, the next time reality presents a situation with the potential for “losing control,” we will not feel so threatened since our consciousness has become accustomed to this condition during daily meditation.

The idea of a control-free life is strange to modern people, sometimes even contradicting everything we have been taught to believe. So, patience is required here, along with a willingness to grow beyond old concepts and beliefs about reality. But the deeper we allow this remarkable process to penetrate our being, the more we discover ourselves as complete human beings. We continue to investigate fear endlessly. As previously stated, it will not vanish as long as we exist in a human body. One of the most remarkable investigators of fear throughout human history was Gautama Buddha. The Buddha identified two fundamental types of fear: The fear of losing what we believe we have. The fear of not obtaining what we believe we lack.

Examine your fears, and you will find that behind them is always one of these two. Why do we go to war? Generally, when do you fight in life? This happens only when you believe you have something that is threatened, something that can be taken away from you. Or when you believe that without a fight, you will not get what you believe you need, want, or deserve—that thing without which you cannot be happy, fulfilled, established, enlightened, etc. Any time you find yourself ready to fight, ask yourself: What are you trying to protect? What is threatened? Is it honor? Respect? Status? Property? Territory? Faith? A set of beliefs? What do you believe you possess that might be taken away? What do you believe you lack that the world might prevent you from having? So, what do we do with this realization? How do we grow beyond these two fundamental fears? Guruji says you are only two steps away from enlightenment. Chant this and be free: I am nothing—I have nothing I am everything—all is mine To achieve total freedom, you need to take only two steps:

Realize you are nothing: Through the process of shedding false identifications, you are left with no more references to yourself. You are left with nothing. Realize you are everything: When there are no more identifications that bind you or fence you in, you expand to include everything. If you are nothing and have nothing, what can be taken away from you? Here, the first fear dissolves. If you are everything, all is yours. What can you still acquire? Here, the second fear dissolves. You are free. A free consciousness is a consciousness that knows: I am not my intellect. The intellect is but the spectator judging the screen of the mind and filling it with meaning Practice: Clear some time for a quiet experience of the Intellect. Take a deep breath in… and let go. Link to a guided meditation about the INTELLECT. The Memory Fifth Level of Existence The memory is not who I am. It is the path on which I have walked up to this moment. The memory is the fifth level of our existence.

Within memory, we store everything we have experienced throughout the years, from the moment we became conscious up to this very moment. We experience a sensation. It is projected on the screen of our mind. The intellect judges it, assigns meaning to it, categorizes it, and so on. Memory takes all of that and stores it in its warehouse. When needed, we return to that warehouse, retrieve the relevant memory, and reuse it—as integrated knowledge, an educational experience, a trauma, or any other form of recycling. Memory takes you from the present to the past Memory plays an important role in our ability to grow, learn, and become wiser. Yet, memory has a tricky nature. When we are preoccupied with memories, longing for a long-gone reality, missing people we once knew, or stuck in a trauma, it is clear that our consciousness has once again escaped the present moment and retreated to what has already passed. Again, we miss the present moment. Memory draws our attention away from the now, preventing full awareness of reality. Memory sticks to the negative

Memory also tends to bring forward the least pleasant experiences from the past. Even if you received 100 applauses for a job well done, the one complaint will likely accompany you to bed. “Why did he say that to me? Everyone else was so pleased with my work. Why did he have to ruin it all…?” When I am preoccupied with my memories, I fixate on what has already happened, usually focusing on the unpleasant aspects. This is always problematic, but especially so when I use memory to construct what I call “My Story” and identify with it. My Story describes the level of identification with the events I have experienced. The chain of events becomes a story, and the degree of my entanglement with it defines it as “mine.” Thus, “My Story” is born. The attachment we develop to our story becomes a significant barrier on the path to true freedom. When the story becomes the answer to the question “Who am I?” the real rollercoaster begins.

Who am I? I am that story! I am a product of that story. In this case, the story almost immediately becomes an excuse. We use it, consciously or unconsciously, as the reason why we are not and cannot be free. “I am so-and-so today because of what happened to me, what I have been through.” When we present ourselves to the world through this story, we soon find that the story pulls us back in time to what happened long ago, sometimes to a prehistoric era: “When I was 3 years old. When I was 5… such and such happened to me back then. That’s why today I am…” The story becomes the reason why I can’t be free. “I am stuck now because when I was a boy, I was scared. Society/ culture/ my parents are the reason I am…” More and more conditionings and excuses accumulate. At this stage, I would encourage you to investigate yourself. Are you using ‘Your Story’ as an excuse? Give yourself examples of when and how this happens.

I hear people say things like: “What you teach is fine for the ashram. In the ashram, you can live like that. But here, it’s irrelevant/ impossible…” So, what do you do? Become a victim of the geography of the story? Your story? Or: “Sure, when I have enough time and money, I can also reflect on these issues, but unfortunately I have too many obligations at this point.” So, what do you do? Become a victim of the bank account status of this story? Your story? A free person knows that their story is just a story—a collection of experiences and events they have had from the moment they became conscious until this very moment. But it is, in no way, who they truly are. It is merely the path they have walked up to this point. Just as a traveler in the woods does not confuse the path they walk on with themselves, a free person does not confuse their life path with who they are.

I do not intend to diminish the influence and importance of the story. Surroundings have significant and meaningful effects on shaping our personality and its driving forces: beliefs, fears, conditionings, etc. Millions of therapists build careers in this very space. But the spiritual path illuminates an important point: the personality and its driving forces are all external wrappings. They only mask and obscure you from yourself, from who you are—the Self that hides behind them all. Sooner or later, when you are brave or desperate enough to begin shedding these external wrappings, you will arrive at the point where you are invited to shed your identification with this story. You are not that story - You are free from it Someone asked a spiritual teacher named Tyuhar, an Israeli who moved to Costa Rica to teach, if he did not feel obligated to teach Israelis back home before going to the other side of the world to teach strangers. His answer was short and precise: “Israel was the origin of my journey.”

So much freedom is contained in these simple words. My homeland is not who I am. It is the starting point of a journey I am on. That origin does not obligate me in any way. I am free to reinvent myself with each new step. I am not bound to a specific agenda, affiliation, or preference for one group over another—more and more beliefs and identifications that this story might entangle me with. If we look back at the history of human conflict, we discover that all conflicts are the product of confused self-identification by the parties involved. When a person identifies themselves primarily as a nationalist or a member of a certain religion and only then as a father, a husband, or a human being, they heighten the sense of separation and alienation. Before you know it, one group starts fighting another group over superficial differences.

When this order of identification resets to something closer to the truth (e.g., first and foremost: “I am a divine entity currently undergoing a human experience. Then, I am a man, a husband, a father, a member of a certain nation, religion, etc.”), we find that at the most basic levels of identification, we are all the same. We are all one. No matter where I live or what I do, we are all fundamentally the same. All conflicts between people and nations will cease when this understanding dawns on humanity. There is likely much more work ahead, but it is good to realize what we are striving for. Another issue related to our story is the sense of ownership we take over it. When I ask people to share some of their story in a group, I repeatedly encounter resistance, embarrassment, and fear. All of these arise from the sense of affiliation we have with this story. That story is who I am. Sharing the story might somehow jeopardize my image. If people don’t like my story, they might not like me (as long as the story defines me). Who will you be without the story?

How can you stop identifying with this story? Whom will you be without it? When participants finally agree to share, one of the most magnificent discoveries is that everyone tells the same story. Of course, the specific details vary—the names, faces, and situations are different—but the underlying structure of the story is the same, retold again and again. We discover that our story is not unique. We are all on the same stage, participating in the same play. Our roles change occasionally. Today I am the hero; tomorrow, I’ll be the villain. Today, I wronged someone; tomorrow, someone will wrong me. Roles change, but the show goes on, and: “All the world’s a stage, and all the men and women merely players.” (William Shakespeare) We are all having the same human experience. When we realize the universality of our story, our identification with it begins to dissolve. That story is no longer mine. It is just another aspect of a much greater human experience.

Years ago, I taught a course in Spain. Towards the end, a middle-aged businessman who participated in the course came to me and said: “Listen, Yaron, everything you teach is very nice, and I would be happy to integrate it into my life, but I have ‘my problems’ that I need to resolve first before I can be available to all of that.” My answer was: “On your path, you will make two discoveries: The first is that these problems are not yours. We are all there, facing the same dilemmas and difficulties. We all fall in and out of love. We all experience hope and despair. We are all challenged by our finances, careers, children, etc. You didn’t invent these problems, and you don’t need to solve them for the sake of humankind. The second discovery will be that these ‘problems’ are not problems at all, only lessons and experiences in time.”

The message here is not, “If so many around me are suffering, then my personal suffering is justified,” but rather, “Observe the drama that attachment to your story creates.” When this “mine” attitude toward “my story” dissolves, you are free to experience it without fear or threat. Then you can fully participate in it. Then it is also easier to offer forgiveness and gratitude. When you recognize the person in front of you as another divine manifestation currently undergoing the human experience, just as you are, what can divide you? What can you want or need from them? What can they take away from you? Wake up and realize: “Your story” is just a story, and it is not who you are. A free consciousness is a consciousness that knows: I am not my story “My story” is just a story, and it is not mine Practice: Clear some time for a quiet experience of the Memory. Take a deep breath in… and let go. Link to a guided meditation about the MEMORY: The Ego Sixth Level of Existence The Ego is not who I am. It is an illusion of separation within me The ego is the sixth level of existence.

The ego is a term loaded with many meanings and interpretations. Countless words have been written about the ego and our complex relationship with it. Originally, Sigmund Freud defined the term “Ego,” along with the other two components of the psychic apparatus: “id” and “superego,” in his structural model of the psyche. However, as a concept, it has existed for ages, reminding us that we still haven't fully grasped the true essence of our self. Before we delve into the age-old questions of whether the ego is good or bad and whether we should cultivate or destroy it, it is helpful to understand what we are actually referring to when we use the word “ego”—a short word with so many interpretations. To establish a unified terminology, let's define “ego” as follows: Ego is the illusion of separation

What do I mean by this? When I feel separate, different; when the situation I am experiencing and I are not aligned as one; when the person in front of me and I are not one and the same, then I am experiencing reality through the sixth level of existence—the ego. The ego prevents the realization of unity. To fully understand the ego, we first need to understand what unity truly means. Unity Until the modern age, approaching the concept of unity often required religious faith. Religion was the primary domain where this term was referenced and explained. “The Lord is one…” is a common description of divinity in many religions.

Divinity was presented as an omnipresent entity or something similar. For secular individuals, access to the concept of unity, especially as an existential experience, was limited. This has been changing in recent decades. A new avenue has opened, allowing secular individuals to connect with the notion of unity. This avenue is, of course, the “secular religion” of science. The overlap between science and religion is one of the most intriguing and dynamic fields of research today. A secular person typically believes that what science determines as fact is truth, either empirically or as an undisputed thesis. Have you ever seen an atom? No, but you trust what you learned in chemistry and understand that matter is made up of molecules and atoms. Therefore, it is valuable to explore what science has to say about unity.

Science describes unity through various observations of nature, not just as a philosophical idea or an ideal described in religious texts, but as a description of the nature of the physical reality we all share and experience. Since we are discussing physical reality, let’s begin with physics and its perspective on this matter. Physics and you

Physics has evolved in three stages. First, there was Newtonian physics, which described the system of forces between objects. What Newton could not explain was what happens to an object at very high speeds, close to the speed of light. The second stage was Einstein’s theory of relativity. This theory made it possible to mathematically describe how an object behaves when moving close to the speed of light and the connection between its mass and its energy. However, scientists then realized that even Einstein’s relativity could not explain the behavior of subatomic particles moving close to the speed of light in experiments conducted in the mid-20th century. This led to a new science with its own theories, mathematics, and rules: Quantum Physics. I will keep this explanation simple and to the point and, of course, explain its connection to unity.

Quantum physics emerged after an experiment where scientists fired photons (light particles) through a narrow slit onto a screen. They discovered that the photons sometimes behaved like waves and sometimes like particles. Trying to understand this strange behavior, they reached a staggering conclusion that stunned the scientific world and changed it forever. The conclusion was that the beam of photons behaves like a wave when the system is closed and there is no direct monitoring of the experiment. But when it is being monitored, it behaves like an assembly of particles. This means that the presence of the observer has an indirect influence on the outcome of the experiment. The beam can behave as a wave (a range of possibilities) or an assembly of particles (a determined state). In summary, the double-slit experiment demonstrated that quantum objects like photons can exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties and that the act of measurement (or any interaction that could provide information about the system) plays a crucial role in determining which behavior is observed.

The implications of this conclusion revolutionized how science explains the world. Quantum physics has continued to evolve and continues to challenge old, sometimes obsolete, ways of thinking with new theories. Today, quantum physics is at the forefront of modern science and is used to describe the behavior of complex physical phenomena that were previously puzzling, such as weather prediction, financial market behavior, and other complex systems operating in uncertain environments and influenced by unpredictable forces. Quantum computers can now deal with dilemmas that would take traditional computers an endless amount of time to solve.

So, how is all of this relevant to our understanding of unity? Quantum physics describes the influence each of us has on our environment. It describes the universe as one living organism in which everything—living, growing, or still—exists in a web of endless relationships with everything else. Quantum physics introduced the concept of the “Butterfly Effect,” a parable that illustrates this point. The butterfly effect suggests that a butterfly flapping its wings on one side of the world can, through a series of escalating chain reactions, cause a hurricane on the other side. If a butterfly can cause such a profound effect without conscious awareness, can we continue to justify the belief that “Whatever we do, it won’t matter anyway…”? We always have an influence. Whether we choose to join a demonstration or stay home and watch it on the news, we have an influence. Whether we act or refrain from acting, we have an influence. Not always in ways we can understand or predict, but our influence is always there, shaping and reshaping reality.

As someone on a spiritual path, the important question is not how you can influence, but what is your motivation for doing so? When the intention to influence comes from a place free of fear and suffering, devoid of personal agendas, and instead arises from peace and inner harmony, the influence will be harmonious and life-affirming. When the intention to influence (or manipulate) comes from a place of internal conflict, stress, and fear, the influence will be disharmonious and against the natural flow of life. This is the true meaning of karma—the law of cause and effect. When you create disharmony by acting from the ego (karma yoga), the universe creates a corrective reaction to return to its balanced state of harmony. This correction is not about reward or punishment. It has nothing to do with human morals or values; it is simply a natural movement of correction back to complete harmony like a wave on a lake creating other waves until the lake returns to its calm state. “Intention creates reality” is not a new-age slogan, but a physical reality

Quantum physics teaches us to recognize our true position in the universe: we are all interconnected, down to our atoms. We are reminded of our responsibility as creators of reality itself. We are the ones influencing the outcomes of the existential experiment. We determine whether our daily reality is a continuum of opportunities for growth or for suffering. The well-known phrase “Intention creates reality” is revealed not just as a hollow new-agey slogan but as a physical reality, whether we like it or not. At this point, I encourage you to try this mindfulness exercise: Investigate your relationship with the reality you experience. Do you adopt a victim’s approach to your surroundings? Give examples. Do you recognize yourself as the creator of that reality? Can you see reality as an expression of your intentions and inner world? Your intention affects the reality you experience, near and far.

During the Lebanon War in the 1980s, a group of 900 meditators gathered along the Israeli-Lebanese border and meditated in 30 collective groups of 30 people from morning to dusk, with the intention of spreading peace and harmony. On that day, the number of violent incidents dropped dramatically, and there were no casualties on either side. In Washington, D.C., one of the most violent cities in the U.S., a similar experiment on a larger scale was conducted one August a few years later. Approximately 4,000 volunteers from around the world spread throughout the city to meditate collectively throughout the month, sending the intention of peace and nonviolence. It was predicted that there would be a 25% drop in violent crime due to the collective intention of the meditators. The Chief of Police said on television that it would take 60 centimeters of snow in August to produce such an effect in his city. But eventually, the local police became a sponsor of the experiment because the level of violent crime did indeed drop by 25% that summer.

You don’t need to travel to Washington, D.C., to experience this effect. In your personal life, you can find that your intention influences your environment. Sometimes you enter a room, and without anyone saying anything, you sense a tense atmosphere. “What just happened?” you ask. “What did I miss?” You can feel it in the air. When Ramadan begins in Muslim countries, Yom Kippur in Israel, Christmas in Christian countries, or Navaratri in India, you can sense a shift in the energy. This is our collective intention influencing the environment. This is also the power of prayer. When a mother asks for an audience to pray for her sick child, that collective prayer has an influence. It makes a difference. Or when visiting a holy place of prayer or meditation, you feel a sense of serenity in the air. The more sensitive you are, the more aware you become of these differences—this unity of consciousness. Influencing is not controlling

It is important to understand that we will not always be able to comprehend exactly how our intentions translate into physical reality. This means we do not have control over reality, but we do influence it. Our collective intention creates reality in every passing moment. Quantum physics brings the responsibility back to you. How would you like to use it? Astronomy and you

Another science that can shed light on unity as the nature of reality is astronomy. From the earliest times, astronomers have tried to answer the fundamental question: Where did all of this come from? How was the universe born? Currently, the prevailing theory regarding the origin of the universe is the Big Bang theory. The Big Bang describes a cosmic event that occurred roughly 13.7 billion years ago. From a single point in the vastness of space, a massive explosion of mass and energy gave birth to everything. Science, of course, does not attempt to explain why such an event occurred. That is not its domain. This is where spirituality enters, describing a divine intention materialized into matter. This will be discussed further in Part II of the book. This massive explosion propelled an immense amount of matter and energy in all directions, which, over time, coalesced into the planets, stars, galaxies, and all other celestial objects we know and will come to know.

So, what does all of this tell us about unity? All matter and energy originated from the same event, at the same time, at the same point. So did you—the matter that constitutes you, the energy that sustains you, comes from there. At the atomic level of your existence, you are one with creation. One with me. Can you see that? Chemistry and you Let us turn to chemistry. The matter your cells are made of—the molecules—all originate from planet Earth, which itself is composed of stardust, the product of countless cycles of stellar birth and death. Your body was initially built from matter and energy flowing in through the umbilical cord—matter your mother received from Earth. Then you arrived on this planet to continue consuming earthly materials: protein, fat, minerals, vitamins, water, and so on. You are a molecular product of Mother Earth. We all are. Once you realize the deeper meaning here, you can never truly feel alone on this planet. You become a true part of it. Unity and You

Unity, then, is the nature of the reality we are all part of—not just a nice idea, but the nature of reality itself. When I do not experience this as an existential reality, it means I am living in an illusion (Maya), a kind of lie, a fictional movie that clouds my vision and prevents me from living up to my full potential. It prevents the full unveiling of the true nature of reality and of myself. There is a story about a wave that illustrates this clearly:

A wave was born in the ocean, like all waves. It rose from the water and took on its own unique shape, like all waves. But by some miraculous event, this particular wave also gained self-consciousness. It became self-aware. This self-awareness obscured the memory of the ocean, as it was aware only of “itself.” Immediately, this sense of separation raised questions within it, such as: “What do I want? What do I need? How can I express my individuality? I want to be yellow! It’s not right for me to be blue like the rest of these waves. To be happy, I need to be yellow. In fact, I’m a nonconformist. To express my individuality, I need to flow towards the deep sea, not towards the shoreline like the others.” The wave is now perpetuating the kinds of ideas that separateness generates. Then, after 30–40 seconds—roughly the lifespan of a wave—while caught up in this existential drama, the wave broke on the shore, just like all the other waves, and returned to the ocean. I vow to dedicate my next book to this topic.

This is the story of all of us. We all originate from unity, receiving our individual expression and self-awareness, which, along with the development of the ego, obscures the sense of unity. We live a full lifespan with an inherent sense of separation, preoccupied with questions the ego generates: “What do I want? What do I need? What will I gain from all of this?” This is the mantra of the ego. And then, after 80–90 years—which, compared to eternity, are not much different from the wave’s 30–40 seconds—we dissolve back and merge with what we originally emerged from and were never truly separate from: unity. What will you gain from all of this? Have you ever truly considered this? What tangible profit will you take from life? Honor? Status? Recognition? Property? What are you striving for? Some say, “At least I will leave my mark on history…” To them, I say, “Honestly, do you remember the name of your great-grandfather? Not even their name… You, too, will disappear into eternity. Nothing will remain.”

We are here to learn how to depart, how to let go and surrender all our crutches. A free person is a person who lets go of this clinging, and knows: I will gain nothing from this in a personal sense. If there is something I can leave behind, it is my contribution to the evolution of universal consciousness. This is not a personal profit, but it is my true contribution. So, the ego is only an illusion of separateness. Even if the wave forgets the ocean, it is still part of it. It derives all its energy and power from it. What would a wave be without the ocean to carry it? Lift the wave 50 centimeters above the ocean, and it will turn into spray and immediately disappear. A wave is an oceanic expression. So are you! You are an inseparable part of unity, of oneness. You can choose to live in this illusion of separateness and dedicate your life to futile attempts to gain something from it, to fill that bottomless pit within you from the outside in, but you will always be an inseparable expression of something much greater than yourself—an expression of eternity, of unity.

The ego is a clever and sophisticated creature. It can use any manipulation to preserve the illusion of itself within you. Its main tool is fear, and the primary fear is the fear of losing control. The ego instills in consciousness all the superstitions that nourish this fear: “Be careful not to lose control. It’s irresponsible, childish. It’s dangerous. You are in danger.” But the truth is that it is in danger. The ego knows that when you agree to let go of the illusion of control, it faces serious, existential danger. We exist in a cage of self-identification, which narrows the space in which we allow ourselves to exist. Within this cage, we maintain the illusion of control. The bars of this cage are made of fears, and the thickest bar of all is the fear of losing control. Only a few of us believe that this cage has a lock. Even fewer are brave or desperate enough to try to open that lock and step out. Those fortunate ones who step out, when looking back at the cage they just left, are awed by an amazing revelation: There is no cage - There never was

But this can only be realized from the outside. When we agree to let go of our need to control, a magical and astonishing event occurs—an event that brings us closer to the seventh level of existence: the Self. A free consciousness realizes: I am not my ego The ego is but an illusion of separateness Practice: Clear some time for a quiet experience of the Ego. Take a deep breath in… and let go. Link to a guided meditation about the EGO: The SELF Seventh Level of Existence The Self is who I am. My inherent nature, beyond all exterior shells We have walked a long path together. Along the way, we agreed to contain, peel away, and grow beyond the first six levels of existence. I am not the body, nor the breath, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor the memory, nor the ego. So, what is left? If I am not all the things I once thought I was, then who am I?

Remain with this mystery. Only a few fortunate or brave individuals dare to reach this point in the journey—agreeing to let go and grow beyond all beliefs and obligations, beyond fears and attachments, to relax in the great mystery of this uncertainty. Who am I? When you agree to let go and relax, you become available to experience the Self.

In that magical moment, we discover that the “I” dissolves into unity. The experience of a separate “me” dissolves into something greater. Then, there is no longer a “me” who needs and wants, a “me” who takes ownership, who succeeds and fails, a “me” who gains any personal benefit. When consciousness agrees to let go and relax, it melts into the present moment and transforms into its expression. You know this from personal experience. This is not an idealistic fantasy. We all have these graceful moments when there is a connection, a merging between the experience and the experiencer—moments where the “doer” dissolves into the action, and the action is simply done. The “I” who enjoyed the sunset dissolves, and a sunset is experienced through what used to be “me.” In those precious moments, we rise beyond space and time. We become, even if fleetingly, hollow and empty, totally available to the experience. And the experience happens through us. Then, we “wake up” with the feeling of: “Wow! What just happened? How long was ‘I’ gone…?”

Then and there, reality is experienced through the Self. You can learn about this type of experience from the story of Suzanne Segal. Suzanne was a remarkable woman who experienced a spontaneous awakening, which she describes in her book, Collision with Infinity. She describes it as a traumatic event where the sensation of a separate self disappeared spontaneously, without preparation or warning. She likened it to a head-on collision with enlightenment. At the time, she was pregnant, and in her book, she describes an existential fear that overwhelmed her: Who is going to be the mother of the baby about to be born? If there is no “me” to take responsibility, what will become of this baby? And then she describes how, miraculously, motherhood simply happened through her. This description alone makes the book worth reading.

Free from the sensation of a separate doer who acts, succeeds, or fails, motherhood unfolded through her. And the baby received everything a baby needs—diapers, breastfeeding, love, and affection. Everything it needed was provided, without any sense of doership. This is an example of existence free from separateness—a life lived from the seventh level of existence: the Self. All the first six levels of existence are experienced with a sense of identification: My body is me; my thoughts are me; my story is me. The seventh level is experienced free of any identification or ownership. The Self is not “mine” simply because when the Self is experienced, it means you have grown beyond the ego, the illusion of separateness. Then there is no “I” that needs to identify itself through an experience or a definition. The Self is not “me” because there is no “I” anymore. The “I” dissolves into something greater, fuller, and more holistic. The wave remembers the ocean. The separated, disengaged space disappears, along with all the superstitions and turbulence it creates within you.

All the forces that once motivated you, based on feelings of need and want, based on the illusion of “There is not enough,” that you still need to gain or protect what you have, all of these disappear from your consciousness (which, by now, is no longer “yours” anyway…). You are free from all wanting and needing. The Self does not want or need. It is connected to abundance. It is an expression of abundance. The motivation that once drove you, springing from a fundamental experience of lack and need, is replaced by a new force—a force that knows abundance, internal wealth. You discover that you are an expression of everything you once wished for, and longed for. You are Peace. You are Joy. You are Love. The fountain cannot be thirsty You discover yourself as the fountain of love. And a fountain cannot be thirsty. That is against its very nature.

Love is not just the emotion we experience in relationships. Often, what we find there has nothing to do with love. It is more like a contract between two suppliers and consumers: “I will give you this, and you will give me that.” From a place of needing and wanting, you connect with a partner who is supposed to fill that hole within you. You become a bookkeeper, afraid of giving more than you receive. Because there is “not enough,” the little you have must be protected. You give love very carefully, only after verifying in advance that you will get it back, with interest! Of course, I may be exaggerating to highlight the absurdity. And when the supplier stops delivering or falls behind on payments, you replace them with another, more promising vendor. The ever-growing divorce rate speaks for itself. An experience of lack and emptiness connects with another experience of lack and emptiness—and thus begins the human drama of relationships.

When you operate from the seventh level, from the Self, you are free from the illusion that you require love simply because you are an expression of that love. Love then reveals itself as your very nature, the nature of reality. Love reveals itself not just as an emotion felt within the context of human relationships. Love reveals itself as the universal force that transforms separation into unity, the life force that sustains creation, and the attractive force that unites everything into one living organism. It is the same force that attracts the electron to the nucleus, the moon to the Earth, the Earth to the sun, the butterfly to the flower, and me to my wife. Ultimately, there is nothing personal about it. It is simply the expression of the Self. Such love has no agenda, no personal interest.

When you operate from the Self, no personal interest guides your choices about whom to give to or how much to give. The fountain of love does not filter or discriminate. It doesn’t say, “I will water only the blond animals…” Any thirsty creature is welcome to drink. The act of drinking justifies the fountain’s very purpose—to share its splendor and grace. So, it is with you. Your ability to give is revealed as your true nature. Every opportunity to share becomes an existential justification. There are no profit/loss calculations, no hidden agendas, and no fear of being taken advantage of. A “sucker” is someone who lives in the constant illusion of a negative give/take balance sheet. In their mind, they always give more than they receive. But when you let go of that mental accounting, you will never feel like a sucker again. It simply ceases to exist. Like the sun, which shines its light and warms its surroundings. The sun does not care if you are sunbathing, enjoying the sunny day, or escaping to an air-conditioned room. It fulfills its purpose—to give light and warmth—no questions asked, no preconditions.

When you operate from the Self, your giving becomes free from conditioning. Have you ever asked yourself what people want from you? What do they really want? What does your spouse want? Your children? Your friends? Your parents? Your colleagues? Deep down, behind all the masks, everyone wants the same thing: for you to love them unconditionally, just as they are. And that is your very nature: unconditional love. As long as you avoid shedding your external layers and diving deep into your true nature, this is what you will also seek from others. This is a kind of cosmic irony: because of a lack of self-awareness, everyone wants from you what you truly are, but because of that same lack of self-awareness, you avoid giving them the one thing that would resolve every drama in your relationships—unconditional love.

An action arising from the Self is performed without a “doer.” You become an expression of love in action (akarma yoga). Your nature is the nature of love, and the nature of love is always to spread, unite, touch, give, and fill. This happens spontaneously, without any intentional direction from you, without a doer. Love knows where to flow, when to flow, and what is empty and needs filling. Alternative healers learn to become hollow and empty so that this healing love can flow through them, whether it is Reiki, other forms of energy healing, or any other healing modality. Spiritual teachers know how to empty their consciousness to allow knowledge to flow. This happens spontaneously, without intervention by a doer. They become a conduit, allowing the process to occur through them. Love is your very nature—the nature of the universal power that transforms separation into unity. A free consciousness is a consciousness that knows: I am Peace I am Joy I am Love Practice: Clear some time for a quiet experience of the Self. Take a deep breath in… and let go.

Link to a guided meditation about the SELF: Part II Q&A on the Path In ancient traditions, knowledge was often shared through dialogues between a disciple and their teacher—a format that allows wisdom to unfold naturally and awaken consciousness. This chapter will be presented as a conversation between a disciple and a teacher, drawn from a series of meetings held by a spiritual circle called the “White Path” between 2007 and 2008. Presented with love. The Meaning of Awakened Consciousness Q: What is the meaning of awakened consciousness? A: Ooooohhh! Consciousness is one of the true wonders this universe has created. Let me answer your question from another perspective. For years, I was troubled by a persistent question that arose in various contexts and prevented peace of mind. I posed this question to every spiritual teacher I met, but no answer truly satisfied me. The question took many forms, such as: “What is the ultimate divine agenda?” “Is it important that more people join the spiritual path?”

“Why does the spiritual path dedicate so much time and effort to persuading us to cease suffering?” “How does all of this assemble into a coherent, meaningful realization?” Years passed, and these questions remained hovering, unanswered. Until, in an instant, the answer revealed itself. It was on a fine night with a round, bright moon and mist covering the valley—just kidding! Do you want the whole story? The story that explains the meaning of our consciousness? Remember: this is just one story. There can be many others, perhaps better told, but this one offers a compelling answer to your question. You may choose to adopt it as a possible explanation. I know I did, and it has helped me on my path. So, the story goes:

13.7 billion years ago, nature/ cosmic consciousness/ oneness/ silence/ God—whatever you wish to call it—decided it reached the evolutionary stage where it was ready to experience itself as matter, to know and learn what it feels like to exist as matter. God has always been there—before time and after time, before this universe was born and after it will cease to exist. God exists. Somewhere in our DNA, we all share this knowledge, don’t we? Nod your heads occasionally so I know you’re still with me, breathing… ☺ At a certain point, the Big Bang occurred, and all the matter and energy we know of, and will come to know, was created. From that moment on, that is what God has been doing: experiencing itself in matter, as matter, as all sorts of matter and energy. But when human consciousness emerged, this experience gained a bonus, an unprecedented added value. Human consciousness could give meaning to the divine existential experience. Q: What do you mean by “meaning”?

A: Consciousness allows for a space of knowing. Through human consciousness, God receives new meaning to the experience of itself as energy and matter—a meaning that had no validation, space, or opportunity to occur until then. That is the meaning of “meaning.” God created this universe to experience itself as energy and matter (which are physically and spiritually the same).
